mobile.intro: Mobile's oldest living landmark grows on a private lot in the Oakleigh Garden District, and its limbs reach out over Caroline Avenue, so the street gets it anyway. The Duffie Oak is put at about 300 years. Downtown, the Boyington Oak stands outside the Church Street Graveyard on the legend of a printer hanged in 1835, and the live oaks of Bienville Square have outlasted a vote to clear them and a hurricane that took six. Across the bay in Daphne, Jackson's Oak carries a legend of its own.
mobile.meta_description: Live oaks of Mobile, Alabama: the 300-year Duffie Oak over Caroline Avenue, the Boyington Oak of a hanging legend, Bienville Square and Jackson's Oak.
mobile.question_meta: Mobile's oldest tree is the Duffie Oak in the Oakleigh Garden District, put at about 300 years. Where it stands, and three more live oaks worth the trip.
mobile.question_answer: The oldest tree in Mobile is usually said to be the Duffie Oak, a southern live oak in the Oakleigh Garden District whose limbs reach out over Caroline Avenue. It is put at about 300 years, an estimate repeated from source to source rather than a ring count. Its girth is disputed too, at 9.42 metres round by the Native Tree Society's figure and about 7.6 by the Mobile Tree Commission's. The trunk stands on a private lot, so you see it from the street. The city's other famous oaks, the Boyington Oak and the oaks of Bienville Square, have no published age at all.
mobile.question_context: Live oaks are hard to date. They grow fast when young, slow down unpredictably and often hollow, so a ring count is rarely possible and most ages are estimates handed down from one account to the next. The Duffie Oak's 300 years is one of those. Alabama listed it among its Famous and Historic Trees in 2003, and it is a stop on the Mobile Tree Commission's Tree Trail, but its trunk is on private ground, so look from the pavement on Caroline Avenue and stay off the lot. The Boyington Oak, outside the Church Street Graveyard, and the oaks of Bienville Square are both downtown and free to see at any hour. Bienville Square lost eleven oaks in 2020, six to Hurricane Sally and five removed by the city afterwards, and has since reopened with younger trees around its edges. Jackson's Oak is across Mobile Bay in Daphne's Village Point Park Preserve, roughly 25 minutes by car, with a trunk about 8.5 metres round and a legend about Andrew Jackson in 1814 that no document confirms.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Mobile?
faq.a: The Duffie Oak in the Oakleigh Garden District, put at about 300 years. That age is an estimate repeated between sources, not a ring count, and no other oak in the city has a published age to compare it with.

faq.q: Can you visit the Duffie Oak?
faq.a: You can see it, from Caroline Avenue, where its limbs reach over the street. The trunk stands on a private lot, so stay on the pavement and do not step onto the property.

faq.q: Is the Boyington Oak inside the cemetery?
faq.a: No. It stands just outside the wall of the Church Street Graveyard, on the edge of Bayou Street, because the wall was moved back after 1900.

faq.q: Did Andrew Jackson really speak under Jackson's Oak?
faq.a: That is the local legend, that he addressed his troops there in 1814 on the way to Pensacola. No document confirms it. The oak itself is real, about 8.5 metres round, in Village Point Park Preserve in Daphne, across the bay from Mobile.

faq.q: What happened to the oaks of Bienville Square?
faq.a: Hurricane Sally brought down six in 2020 and the city removed five more that October. The square closed for repairs and has reopened, with younger trees planted around its edges. Which survivor is the biggest has not been recorded.

baton-rouge.intro: The oak at the corner of Louisiana's Old State Capitol grounds was already standing when the capitol went up beside it in 1847, and by one estimate it is nearly twice the building's age. It has outlasted the fire of 1862 and the government's move out in 1932, and it still shades the lawn by Repentance Park. Out on Highland Road, the LSU Hilltop Arboretum keeps its own great live oak at its centre, the one couples book for their weddings.
baton-rouge.meta_description: Two live oaks in Baton Rouge: the oak older than the Old State Capitol it shades, and the wedding oak at the heart of LSU Hilltop Arboretum.
baton-rouge.question_meta: Baton Rouge's oldest documented tree is the live oak at the Old State Capitol, put at 230 to 300 years. Where it stands, and one more worth the drive.
baton-rouge.question_answer: The oldest documented tree in Baton Rouge is the live oak at the corner of the Old State Capitol grounds, beside Repentance Park on the downtown riverfront. Country Roads magazine puts it at roughly 300 years and about five metres round; a visitors' waymark says about 230. Neither comes from a ring count, but both put it ahead of the capitol, built between 1847 and 1849. The other great oak in town, the wedding tree at LSU Hilltop Arboretum, has no published age beyond the Live Oak Society's Centenarian class, a hundred years or more.
baton-rouge.question_context: The two ages for the Old State Capitol oak, 230 and 300 years, are both estimates, and live oaks are hard to date. They grow fast when young and slow unpredictably later, so a girth of about five metres fits a wide range of ages. Either figure means the tree saw the capitol built, saw fire gut its interior in 1862, and saw the state government leave for the new capitol in 1932. It should not be confused with the Thomas Boyd oak at the new State Capitol, which fell in Hurricane Gustav in 2008. The Old State Capitol is now a museum, closed on Sundays and Mondays, and the oak stands on the grounds by Repentance Park, a short walk from the River Center. The second tree is a drive away, at LSU Hilltop Arboretum on Highland Road, open free every day in daylight. Its own university gives two different sizes for it, a diameter of 8 feet on one page and 17 on another, so its size is an open question. It is named for Emory Smith, who began the arboretum in 1929.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Baton Rouge?
faq.a: The live oak at the corner of the Old State Capitol grounds is the oldest with a published estimate, roughly 230 to 300 years depending on the source. Neither figure comes from a ring count.

faq.q: Is the Old State Capitol oak the one that fell in Hurricane Gustav?
faq.a: No. The oak lost in Gustav in 2008 was the Thomas Boyd oak at the new State Capitol. The Old State Capitol oak, by Repentance Park, still stands.

faq.q: Can you visit the wedding tree at Hilltop Arboretum?
faq.a: Yes. LSU Hilltop Arboretum on Highland Road is open to the public free of charge during daylight hours, seven days a week. The tree is the arboretum's focal point, and the office, open Tuesday to Friday, can point you to it.

lafayette-louisiana.intro: The Live Oak Society was founded in 1934 by a Lafayette college president who had planted oaks to welcome the twentieth century, and one of its charter members still stands downtown. The Cathedral Oak, put at more than 450 years, may be the reason the cathedral stands where it does. Stephens' own Twentieth Century Oaks, planted on New Year's Day 1901, line the walkways of the university he led. And half an hour away in St. Martinville, the Evangeline Oak stands on Bayou Teche for a love story.
lafayette-louisiana.meta_description: Live oaks of Lafayette, Louisiana: the Cathedral Oak, put at over 450 years, the Twentieth Century Oaks of 1901 and the Evangeline Oak of St. Martinville.
lafayette-louisiana.question_meta: Lafayette's oldest tree is the Cathedral Oak, put at more than 450 years and fenced since 1995. Where it stands, and two more live oaks worth the trip.
lafayette-louisiana.question_answer: The oldest tree in Lafayette is the St. John Cathedral Oak, a southern live oak on the grounds of the Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist downtown. Lafayette Travel and the 100oaks blog put it at more than 450 years, the cathedral reckoned it about 275 years old in 1821, and Waymarking says 500. None of those is a ring count. Arborist Jim Foret measured the trunk at 29 feet 6 inches round in 2015, about nine metres. It was a charter member of the Live Oak Society in 1934 and has been fenced since 1995, so you see it from the cathedral grounds.
lafayette-louisiana.question_context: Lafayette is where the Live Oak Society began. Dr Edwin L. Stephens, first president of what is now the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, founded it in 1934 as a register whose members are trees, with dues of 25 acorns a year. The Cathedral Oak was one of its 43 charter members, and Stephens put it at the top of his Live Oak Trail tours. Ages for it range from about 450 to 500 years, all estimates, and its girth has been measured several times, from 19 feet in about 1929 to 29 feet 6 inches in 2015, a jump that is partly a matter of how people measured. Stephens' own Twentieth Century Oaks are young by comparison, planted on New Year's Day 1901, and eight to ten of the original eighteen still stand near Girard Hall on campus. They are worth the walk for the history rather than the size. The Evangeline Oak is a day trip, about half an hour by car to St. Martinville, where a state plaque links it to the real-life couple behind Longfellow's Evangeline. Nobody has published its age or girth.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Lafayette?
faq.a: The St. John Cathedral Oak, on the grounds of the Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist. Estimates run from more than 450 to 500 years. None comes from a ring count.

faq.q: Can you get close to the Cathedral Oak?
faq.a: It has been fenced since 1995 to protect the roots, so you see it from the cathedral grounds along the fence. There is no charge.

faq.q: Are the Twentieth Century Oaks old?
faq.a: Not by live oak standards. Edwin Stephens planted eighteen of them on New Year's Day 1901, so they are about 125 years old, and eight to ten survive. The reason to visit is that Stephens went on to found the Live Oak Society.

faq.q: How far is the Evangeline Oak from Lafayette?
faq.a: It stands in St. Martinville, on Bayou Teche, about half an hour by car southeast of Lafayette. Evangeline Oak Park is free and run by the city.
